Reality is, I 100% agree, group switching costs is a real moat. That's why we both invested in @TownAI! On the solo side the bar is definitely not as high, but giving one app my passwords, credit cards, and personal information, requires trust -- while it's not "hard" to switch, is something people won't want to do... quote:
Here is my experience setting up @TownAI , Instinct @noahrshinn , and Muse, all at roughly the same time.

Town has a great setup and walks you through the whole thing very smoothly. It's also very powerful, and you can communicate with it through the app, through different messaging apps, through email. It's very powerful, and you can interface with it in a lot of ways.

With that said, when I try to multitask through WhatsApp on Town, it drops the ball a lot. Also, you blow through credits fast on this thing. I would call Town high-end, but expensive. If I were to use it as my daily driver, I would not only need the $200/month plan, I'd probably have to be buying extra credits.

Instinct is getting hyped a lot right now by people trying to make money off it, IMO. At first, it doesn't feel as powerful as something like Town, but the more I use it, the more I like it. I'm on Android, so I only communicate with it through WhatsApp. For the time being, it's free, and there is no paid version. It has a lot of horsepower behind it. They must be spending a boatload on tokens right now, and that can't last forever without charging customers.

On one level, Instinct doesn't feel as powerful and multidimensional as Town, but on another level, its simplicity and elegance is really nice. I like how casual it feels, and it's deceptively powerful.

Muse has an incredible amount of horsepower behind it. I gave it two very intensive tasks, and it moved through them very quickly. Also, integrations are really smooth. It learns super fast, and you can throw a lot at it. They must be using a lot of compute on this right now, and it's a good value for the money right now, meaning there's a free plan and if you want to upgrade, there's a $20/month plan and a $100/month plan. My sense is it's a better value than Town, at least right now, but all of that can change in the future.

I want to give an honorable mention to @TaskletAI . I see it in a very similar way to Town, just not as dressed up and polished, but their $25/month plan is a pretty good value, especially if you use Luna with it. You can get a lot done at a low cost.

There seems to be a frantic race to see who's going to be the AI agent of choice. My personal favorite is still Hermes @NousResearch and I also have a ChatGPT Pro and @perplexity_ai Max plan. I'm not a fan of Perplexity Computer, but I like the other features of the Max plan. The ChatGPT work app is super impressive, and I like how I can use my OAuth account with Hermes. I would say, as a non-coder, I get my best work done with the ChatGPT work app with either Sol or Astra.

I have yet to try Grok @bot , but probably will be doing their 3-month trial soon. Based on what I've seen of it, it feels like a dressed-up version of Tasklet, as it's essentially a VPS, but it's looking like Grok 4.7 could be at Astra level, which is why I want to give it a try.

There are so many options right now, it's insane. It's going to be really interesting to see who are going to be the winners in this race.

quote:
My biggest takeaways from Jean-Denis Greze (@jgreze), co-founder of @TownAI:

1. Experience buys you a 5–10% better shot, not a different game. Network, easy fundraising, knowing how to scale a team — all real, all marginal. "Are you cut out to be a founder? I don't think you find out until you try to do it."

2. Every startup is just convincing humans to want a thing that doesn't exist. That collapses founder anxiety into two things you control: what you sell and how you sell it. "There's no law of physics. It's literally just humanity."

3. A working business isn't the same as a winnable one. His tax product hit high six figures in 12 months with happy customers — but businesses switch preparers once a year, so word of mouth couldn't compound. Check what your market's shape permits before you grade execution.

4. A correct technology bet is worthless without a go-to-market bet attached. They were more convinced than ever that AI could automate tax prep. What they lacked was a reason automation would win them the market faster than it shrank the market.

5. If you no longer believe, staying is the dishonest option. The hard part was the engineers, the partners, admitting failure. But if the founder doesn't believe, keeping people there is what's actually unfair to them. Then run it clean — long severance, help finding jobs.

6. Ship the ugly version to twenty people and let retention tell you. Town launched as a blue "sign in" button on an unstyled page. Twenty people stayed, one running 200 workflows a day. That was enough to redirect the company. Polish came after retention.

7. At a big company, take the important job nobody cool wants. At Dropbox, cool was the desktop client; getting people to pay was not. Easy wins, no exec wrecking your roadmap, a board that loved the revenue. Then make it fun — his team became Team Cash, in red tracksuits.

8. Collect peers in your exact cohort instead of mentors above you. People at your growth rate, comparing real notes, beat looking up to anyone you don't know. Same for your board: the value is the intro to the founder who made this call last year.

9. Under-betting is the real risk when the market moves this fast. A peer told him to stop playing one move at a time and assume the next three all work. "I need to be more overconfident than I am today if we're really going to win."

Full conversation: https://t.co/9lgDIQxRwF

quote:
AI / @TownAI  tips for recruiters:

Was thinking about all my recruiter pals out there who do superhuman work managing processes that don’t follow clean templates (e.g., scheduling around everyone's calendar constraints, engaging a maybe-ghosting candidate, offer to prep) with context split across inboxes, LinkedIn, spreadsheets, Slack, Drive, your ATS etc. Some ways a Townie can help:

1. Interview scheduling

Navigating calendars to schedule interviews for candidates always takes more brain capacity than it should. You can’t just look for open calendar spots b/c one person has a lunch rule, another wants their first day back from PTO left clear, and every on-site round needs its own room. A Townie can do all this for you. prompt to set it up:

>> “When I schedule interviews for a candidate, build around each interviewer's real constraints, not just open calendar slots. Pull those from our hiring Slack channel and past emails too: no one booked their first day back from PTO, a room for every on-site round, each person's own lunch rule. Reuse the exact invite wording I've already approved, no paraphrasing. Confirm the constraints with me first, then run it on one open req as a test."

2. Post-offer approval logistics

Once an offer is approved, closing the candidate consists of things like generating an offer, scheduling follow-ups, updating the ATS, keeping the hiring manager in sync, all while accounting for the candidate’s timeline. A Townie can help! Prompt to set it up:

>> "Once an offer is approved for a candidate, handle the post-offer approval logistics for me. Generate the offer summary, schedule the follow-ups around the candidate's own stated decision date pulled from the recruiter-screen notes and our email threads, keep their stage in my ATS current as things move, and post an update to the hiring manager in Slack at each step. Confirm the follow-up timing and who to notify with me first, then run it on one open offer as a test."

3. Candidate responses and check-ins

Candidate replies come in sporadically throughout the day across email and LinkedIn, and each one needs a next step that fits where that person sits in the pipeline. A Townie can work through the replies, check each candidate's stage and req in the ATS, and draft the next message in the tone already used with that specific person, so a recruiter opens the day to a stack of ready-to-send replies instead of a cold inbox. Prompt to set it up:

>> "Each morning, build me a candidate-reply queue. Go through the overnight replies from candidates in my active pipeline across email and LinkedIn, check each person's stage and req in my ATS, and draft the next message in the tone I've already used with them. Leave anything ambiguous or high-stakes for me to review. Confirm which pipelines to cover with me first, then run it as a test on tomorrow morning's replies."

quote:
Today I walk with @jgreze, co-founder and CEO of @TownAI, an AI on-ramp platform for individuals and businesses. Jean-Denis is the former CTO of @Plaid, led engineering through a blocked $5.3B Visa acquisition, and walked away from the C-suite at 45 to start over from zero, and now he's turned a scrapped AI tax-prep startup into a $55M Series A company backed by Andreessen Horowitz(@a16z). He gets into the week he decided to kill a business that was actually working, and why he refuses to call Town an "AI assistant."

We get into:

- Why he waited until 45, after seven years as Plaid's CTO, to become a founder for the first time

- The week he and his co-founder killed a working, revenue-generating tax-prep startup because it wasn't going to be a rocket ship

- Town's real bet: not a smarter AI assistant, but an onboarding layer that gets normal people leverage from AI without writing a single prompt

- His "accelerators, table stakes, foundations" framework for staying ahead of OpenAI, Gemini, and Google

- Why turning "uncool" work into cult culture, from Dropbox's Team Cash to Plaid's colourful tights, built teams that stuck around

so much more!

Link in comments!

quote:
A friend is remodeling her home right now, and I've had front row seats to all the headaches that come with that (iykyk). I got her set up with a few @TownAI routines that have made the process a little more manageable that I thought I'd share here:

1. A weekly check-in that nudges her contractor when something stalls

Work was drifting and her contractor would go quiet. Now her Townie watches her inbox and her running notes file (Google Doc), gives short weekly reads on where things stand, and nudges her with a pre-drafted email to her contractor. Setup prompt:

>> "Watch my email thread with my contractor and my running renovation notes doc in Google Docs, and give me a short weekly summary of where things stand: what's done, what's next, and anything I owe them a reply on. If they've gone quiet for more than a few days on something I'm waiting on, draft me a follow-up email to them so I can send it with one look. Tell me what you think the open items are first, then start the weekly check-in."

2. Compare bids side by side

She would get 3+ quotes in 3+ formats and couldn't tell which was actually cheaper or what each one leaves out. Her Townie now reads each bid they come in and lines them up: scope, price, timeline, payment schedule, and what's included versus excluded. Setup prompt:

>> "I'm collecting bids from contractors for my home renovation. Each time I forward you a quote or estimate, pull out the scope, total price, timeline, payment schedule, and what's included versus excluded, and add it to a comparison table next to the other bids. Point out where they differ and what looks missing from each one. Ask me what matters most to me first, then show me a draft."

3. Log every decision so nothing gets lost

Renovations are hundreds of micro-decisions: paint, tile, fixtures, appliances. It was hard for her to remember what / why she picked something. Her Townie now has the running record. Setup prompt:

>> "Keep a log of every choice I make for my renovation. When I tell you or forward you a selection (paint color, tile, fixture, appliance), record the room, the item, the brand and model, where it's from, the price, and a quick note on why I picked it, organized by room. Ask me which rooms we're doing first, then set it up."

quote: Town is a credible AI work assistant, not a dressed-up chatbot. It learns context from your email, calendar, documents, messages, and connected business tools; gives its "Townie" an @town.com address; and can send email, schedule meetings, research people, prepare briefings, and run custom routines. Its strongest fit is a busy professional who wants one ambient assistant across work. Its biggest tradeoffs are credit-based pricing and a one-assistant model that is less clean than specialized agents for distinct business processes.
author: UseCarly
notes: Evidence-based buying analysis (not months-long trial); notes Outlook now live post-June launch.

quote: Town.com offers a unique email-native AI assistant that provides users with a dedicated @town.com email address, allowing you to interact with your AI assistant the same way you would a human executive assistant. ... If your work lives across Slack, project management tools, and CRM systems, the email-first model may add friction instead of cutting it.
